title: Culture & Methods Trends 2026: The Human Side of AI Engineering
gist: A seven-person InfoQ practitioner panel argues that 2026's binding constraint on AI-assisted software is not model capability but human throughput: GitHub is projected to go from ~1B to ~14B pull requests in a year, code review and QA processes are breaking, teams are collapsing into one-person-plus-agents units, and nobody fully owns the resulting systems. The recurring investable thesis is that organisations which never embedded agile fundamentals (fast feedback, observability, outcome measurement) will fail catastrophically at AI, creating a widening haves/have-nots gap and demand for guardrail, harness, quality and FinOps/energy-accounting tooling.

themes.theme: AI Adoption Maturity and Risk Calibration

insights.claim: Enterprise AI adoption in 2026 is being run as an all-or-nothing decision rather than being risk-tiered per system, and the fix is to reapply pre-AI risk/impact/context reasoning to decide how much AI belongs in each specific piece of software.
insights.speaker: Vanessa Formicola
insights.so_what: Vendors and internal platform teams selling per-workload AI risk tiering and maturity assessment have an unserved gap; blanket 'AI everywhere' rollouts are the ones most likely to produce visible failures.
insights.quote: I feel that these days is more everything or nothing in the AI space

insights.claim: The appropriate amount of human-in-the-loop should vary by the risk class of the software being built, so organisations need explicit maturity frameworks for AI acquisition rather than a single company-wide policy.
insights.speaker: Vanessa Formicola
insights.so_what: Expect procurement and audit requirements to shift toward per-application AI risk classification, favouring tooling that can enforce differentiated review policies.

insights.claim: The binding constraint on AI adoption is organisational capability rather than tool maturity: people must be capable enough to work with AI while still feeling psychologically safe enough to raise problems they see.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Failure modes in AI rollouts will show up as silence and unreported defects, not as loud incidents — leading indicators are cultural, not technical.
insights.locator: Psychological Safety in the AI Era

insights.claim: AI usage is rising while trust in AI outputs is falling, a contradiction that reframes the engineer's job as building the systems and guardrails that raise the trust factor rather than producing the code itself.
insights.speaker: Yinka Omole
insights.so_what: The spend shift is from code-generation seats toward verification, eval and guardrail infrastructure — trust tooling is the bottleneck layer to own.
insights.quote: a lot more people are adopting AI usage, but fewer people are trusting the outputs, which a really interesting contradiction
insights.locator: The Role of the Engineer is Changing

insights.claim: Teams must decide up front whether a system is being built for humans or for machines, because that choice determines how many humans and which human skills the system will need for its whole life, not just at launch.
insights.speaker: Vanessa Formicola
insights.so_what: A reusable screening question for evaluating any AI-native engineering org: was the maintenance model chosen deliberately or emergently?
insights.quote: building software for humans is different than writing software for machines

insights.claim: Hyper-generating an entire system that nobody in the organisation understands is a risk factor that backfires quickly, so companies should be explicit about how they plan to manage AI-produced systems before shrinking teams or hyper-automating.
insights.speaker: Vanessa Formicola
insights.so_what: Watch for a 2026-2027 cohort of companies forced to re-hire senior engineers to rescue unowned AI-generated codebases.

themes.theme: Code Volume Explosion and Cognitive Load

insights.claim: GitHub pull request volume is projected to rise from roughly one billion per year to about 14 billion per year in 2026, a 14x increase in review load that existing engineering processes were never designed to absorb.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: A 14x jump in review artifacts is a direct TAM signal for code review, static analysis, test generation and provenance tooling — and a load/cost signal for GitHub itself.
insights.quote: I saw recently that GitHub is going from I think one billion pull requests per year to something expected 14 billion pull requests per year predicted for 2026 from one billion last year.

insights.claim: A figure circulating in the engineering community pairs a 300% increase in code volume with a 400% increase in bugs, implying AI code generation degrades defect density rather than merely scaling output.
insights.speaker: Shane Hastie
insights.so_what: If bugs scale faster than code, the marginal value of AI codegen is captured downstream by QA, observability and incident tooling, not by the codegen vendor.
insights.quote: 300% more code, 400% more bugs going hand in hand

insights.claim: The pull request review process is structurally obsolete under AI-scale output because a human reviewer cannot actually read all the code an agent generates.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: Any 2026 engineering process still gated on human line-by-line PR review is a false control; look for orgs replacing it with property tests, harnesses and formal constraints.
insights.quote: Can you really read all the code that AI generates?

insights.claim: Quality assurance independence is collapsing because the same AI system that writes the code is also writing the tests and running the DevOps pipeline that ships it.
insights.speaker: Craig Smith
insights.so_what: Correlated failure across build, test and deploy is an underpriced operational risk; independent verification layers become a compliance requirement, not a nice-to-have.
insights.quote: Is the same machine that just built the same engine that is also testing to the same machine that is also now doing the DevOps that gets it out there?
insights.locator: The Gap Between Haves and Have-Nots

insights.claim: AI-generated artifacts are spawning recursive AI consumption inside organisations — a colleague sends a 47-page AI-written document that the recipient then feeds to AI for a summary — destroying the signal that human-authored communication used to carry.
insights.speaker: Craig Smith
insights.so_what: Internal communication volume is inflating without information gain; productivity metrics based on artifact counts are now actively misleading.
insights.quote: So we've got AI helping us with the AI, and then AI is helping us with the AI again forward outcome.

insights.claim: Harvard Business Review's word of the year was 'work slop' — AI-generated content that makes work harder for people further down the value stream — and the software equivalent is code slop.
insights.speaker: Shane Hastie
insights.so_what: A named, mainstream-business-press concept for AI output externalities signals the start of buyer scrutiny on AI-generated deliverable quality.
insights.quote: Harvard Business Review last year's word of the year was work slop
insights.locator: Defining Value When Code is Abundant

insights.claim: Running multiple parallel agent workstreams forces engineers into constant context switching across abstract concepts — a cost humans have always paid badly — so the productivity gain from parallel agents is partly illusory and its long-term effect on engineer capability is unknown.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Headline agent-parallelism productivity claims should be discounted for context-switch drag; tools that handle cognitive load (orchestration, choice narrowing) capture real value.
insights.quote: you're just stretched across two abstract concepts and you're trying to context switch between them, which we've always sucked at, which has always got the high cost

insights.claim: Different engineers get materially different results from the same AI models because some know what to look for in the output while others trust their sessions heavily, introducing unmeasured risk variance across a team.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Per-engineer output quality variance widens under AI, so aggregate team velocity metrics hide where the real defect risk sits.

insights.claim: Jim Highsmith's formulation that organisations which failed at agile will fail catastrophically at AI is being endorsed by practitioners as the central predictor of who gets value from agentic engineering.
insights.speaker: Shane Hastie
insights.so_what: Prior delivery-practice maturity, not AI budget, is the screening variable for which enterprises convert AI spend into outcomes.
insights.quote: If you failed at agile, you will fail catastrophically at AI
insights.locator: Agility as Foundation for AI Success

insights.claim: Bigger AI-generated change sets raise per-deployment risk, so organisations that skipped fast feedback loops, observability and shift-right practices cannot safely ship agentic output and must retrofit that maturity first.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Observability and progressive delivery vendors are direct beneficiaries of AI codegen adoption — the risk has to land somewhere.
insights.locator: Agility as Foundation for AI Success

insights.claim: A widening haves/have-nots gap is forming between organisations that embraced agility and those still building software the way it was built in 1995, who are now layering AI practices on top of unreformed delivery.
insights.speaker: Craig Smith
insights.so_what: Dispersion in AI-driven productivity outcomes across incumbents will be wide, not uniform — an argument against treating AI adoption as a sector-wide margin tailwind.
insights.quote: still building it on organizations that are still tending software's being built in 1995
insights.locator: The Gap Between Haves and Have-Nots

insights.claim: Most organisations never went back to measure whether shipped features solved the customer problem long before AI existed, and AI now lets them commit that failure at far greater scale.
insights.speaker: Shawna Martell
insights.so_what: Outcome-measurement and experimentation platforms gain urgency as unvalidated shipping volume rises; feature velocity alone becomes a worthless KPI.
insights.quote: They ship something, but they maybe never went back to actually understand if it solved the problem that they had.
insights.locator: Defining Value When Code is Abundant

insights.claim: Engineering orgs are running huge token spend on models that are heavily subsidised by upstream providers, coupling themselves to an economics that may not persist, which makes FinOps discipline and a forward plan as important as ever.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Practitioner-level awareness that inference pricing is subsidised implies repricing risk for AI-dependent software margins; watch contract structures and token cost pass-through.
insights.quote: We're using models and capabilities that are very heavily subsidized by providers upstream.

insights.claim: Much of what is being marketed as new AI engineering practice — harness engineering, guardrails, spec-driven development — is a rebranding of pre-existing methods like static analysis, so studying prior practice is the fastest route to enabling AI-era teams.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Discount novelty premiums on 'AI-native' dev tooling that is repackaged static analysis and CI; the moat is distribution, not the technique.
insights.quote: there are practices that we've had to date that have been rebranded

themes.theme: Team Topologies Collapsing to One-Person Units

insights.claim: The two-pizza team is becoming a one-pizza team: two people plus an AI tool or a swarm of agents is emerging as the default delivery unit.
insights.speaker: Shane Hastie
insights.so_what: Per-seat software pricing models face headcount compression in engineering orgs even as compute spend rises — a mix shift from seats to usage.
insights.quote: What I'm seeing is that two pizza teams becoming a one pizza team. Two people and an AI tool or a swarm of agents.

insights.claim: Team topology is bifurcating by risk: business-critical systems keep a conventional team supercharged by agents, while low-risk software collapses to a product manager plus one developer, with agents as team members in some configurations and all-agent teams in others.
insights.speaker: Vanessa Formicola
insights.so_what: Headcount reduction will be concentrated in low-risk product surfaces, not uniformly across engineering — a filter for reading company layoff narratives.

insights.claim: Mark Anderson's framing of the standoff between engineers, product and design is resolving into a single class of 'builders', with product and design staff committing code while engineers retreat to providing primitives, architecture and APIs.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: If non-engineers ship code, seat expansion for dev tooling moves outside engineering while internal platform/API teams become the durable engineering function.
insights.quote: So now we really just have this one class of people which he's calling just builders. So we're all builders now.
insights.locator: Blurring Roles: We're All Builders Now

insights.claim: The team itself is no longer the right unit of organisational design; the question worth optimising is how to make collaboration more effective in whatever form it takes, including one person plus an agent.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for assessing engineering orgs: stop scoring team structure, score collaboration throughput and information flow.
insights.quote: The thing is how can we make collaboration more effective in the organization? That's where our focus should be.
insights.locator: Blurring Roles: We're All Builders Now

insights.claim: Organisations are consolidating small teams into 25-30 person groups that are actually collections of independent one-person teams whose members hide the fact that an agent is doing the work, so standups surface unrelated updates rather than collaboration.
insights.speaker: Craig Smith
insights.so_what: Reported team sizes now overstate actual collaboration; concealed agent usage also means official AI adoption metrics understate real usage.
insights.quote: But they're all little one person inside a big team.

insights.claim: One-person teams strip out the social reason people show up to work, and agents are not a substitute for the enjoyment of working with other people — a retention risk organisations are not pricing.
insights.speaker: Shawna Martell
insights.so_what: Attrition and engagement, not velocity, are the metrics that will expose over-atomised engineering orgs first.
insights.quote: I can't imagine feeling that way about an agent.

insights.claim: The engineer-manager pendulum is swinging back with managers returning to writing code and shipping features, and role lines are blurring inside engineering too, dissolving the front end / backend / infrastructure / platform separations.
insights.speaker: Yinka Omole
insights.so_what: Engineering management layers thin out; expect flatter orgs and fewer pure-management roles in AI-forward companies.
insights.locator: Blurring Roles: We're All Builders Now

insights.claim: Engineers are shifting from contributors to custodians, with more of the job becoming platform engineering — building the platforms agents write code on, and the review systems that let colleagues contribute safely.
insights.speaker: Yinka Omole
insights.so_what: Internal developer platform and agent-infrastructure budgets rise even where headcount falls — the durable spend line in an AI-native engineering org.
insights.quote: engineers are becoming a lot more custodians rather than just contributors
insights.locator: The Role of the Engineer is Changing

insights.claim: The magic of teams — different viewpoints, different expertise, mutual challenge — is lost when teams degenerate into a set of one-person teams working on completely independent projects.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: Design-quality regressions from lost peer challenge will show up as architectural drift, not as immediate defects — a lagging, hard-to-detect cost.

themes.theme: Junior Pipeline and the Judgment Gap

insights.claim: A tax company's attempt to vibe-code a from-zero rebuild of a tax system with less experienced engineers failed, and a senior developer is being brought in to take over the build.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Early, concrete evidence that AI-first greenfield rebuilds by junior teams fail in regulated domains — a rescue-consulting demand signal.
insights.quote: someone was talking to me about a gig recently with a tax company that had tried to vibe code, rebuild of a tax system
insights.locator: Junior Engineers in the AI Age

insights.claim: AI is a force multiplier in both directions: it amplifies a senior engineer's judgment into extraordinary output and equally amplifies a junior's lack of judgment into output that is not what they wanted.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: AI productivity gains accrue disproportionately to firms with deep senior benches — a differentiator between otherwise similar software companies.
insights.quote: if you're a senior and you have good judgment and you have good experience, AI is like this massive force multiplier

insights.claim: Within six to twelve months the only skill that will matter is how well an engineer can use and corral AI agents, at which point younger engineers with more mental plasticity will out-perform experienced seniors.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: A testable near-term call that inverts the current senior-advantage consensus; if right, seniority premiums in engineering compensation compress fast.
insights.quote: then I think really the only skill that will be important is how well can you use AI? How well can you corral all of these agents working for you?

insights.claim: Senior engineers coaching models are investing in something that lacks a junior's plasticity: you can tell a model once and set a guardrail in stone, but it never internalises the generalised judgment a human would develop, so continued investment in juniors is necessary.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Companies cutting junior hiring are trading a compounding human asset for a non-compounding one — a multi-year talent-supply risk.
insights.quote: but that plasticity isn't there
insights.locator: Junior Engineers in the AI Age

insights.claim: Steve Yegge's framing casts junior engineers as gatekeepers validating incoming work from UX and product against scalability and integration bars — a role that actually sits above where juniors historically started.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: If the entry-level job now requires judgment previously earned over years, the junior-to-senior pipeline breaks at the entry point, not the middle.
insights.quote: which was around the juniors being almost gatekeepers for work coming in from UXers, from product, to validate that those are hitting the bar of scalability
insights.locator: Junior Engineers in the AI Age

insights.claim: The industry is regressing to rockstar and tiger-team language it had already rejected, and because every individual works with an agent whose knowledge is drawn from the same corpus as their neighbour's, the diversity of thought that made teams valuable is being erased.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Homogenised agent-derived solutions imply industry-wide convergence on the same architectures and the same latent failure modes — a correlated systemic risk.
insights.quote: You've got the individual working with a agent that's knowledge is built from the same corpus as every other person sitting next to them and that personal diversity is going to be lost in all of it.
insights.locator: Junior Engineers in the AI Age

insights.claim: Junior learning timelines will compress because implementation fundamentals like writing good Java or C are no longer as necessary, freeing mental bandwidth for structuring questions and spotting technical debt, and individuals are becoming leads very quickly by directing agents.
insights.speaker: Yinka Omole
insights.so_what: Time-to-lead shortens, so engineering seniority ladders and compensation bands will need rebasing; the skill being priced changes from implementation to direction.
insights.locator: Junior Engineers in the AI Age

insights.claim: Getting T-shaped was historically a journey of initiation, failure and success, so the ability to conjure working software with a prompt does not confer the judgment to know whether it will scale or be maintainable in two years.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Maintainability of AI-generated systems built by low-experience teams is the underpriced liability to look for in software diligence.
insights.quote: So being able to cast your wand and have something working will not always give you the judgment of being able to decide if this thing will scale, if this thing will be maintainable in two years.
insights.locator: Junior Engineers in the AI Age

insights.claim: A principal engineer in fintech reports not having written code by hand in months and argues AI will not fundamentally change career paths, because leaders were never selected for writing the best code but for vision, judgment and knowing where to pivot.
insights.speaker: Shawna Martell
insights.so_what: A direct counter to the 'AI rewrites the engineering ladder' narrative — the panel's own senior IC says the selection criteria are unchanged.
insights.quote: I haven't written code by hand in months now.

insights.claim: The distinctions between architect, developer, tech lead, engineering manager, backend and front end are now dead, and engineering maturity should be measured by breadth of skills rather than the depth of a T-shape.
insights.speaker: Vanessa Formicola
insights.so_what: Specialist-only engineers face market obsolescence; hiring, levelling and comp frameworks built on role specialisation are due for a shakeup.
insights.quote: all those categorization that people used to give themselves, they should have been dead before, but they're definitely dead now

insights.claim: The new productivity metric for an engineer should be how much they can be accountable for using all available tools, not how much they can ship — a reframing that directly bounds how far one-person teams and hyper-automation can go.
insights.speaker: Vanessa Formicola
insights.so_what: An actionable substitute for velocity/lines-of-code metrics in an AI-native org; accountability surface area is the real capacity ceiling.
insights.quote: Not much I can ship, but how much can I be accountable using all the tools that I have at my disposal?

insights.claim: Organisations struggled with engineering career paths long before AI existed, and AI has exacerbated rather than created that problem.
insights.speaker: Shawna Martell
insights.so_what: Attributing 2026 career-ladder chaos purely to AI misdiagnoses it; the fix is the same career-architecture work that was already overdue.
insights.quote: AI has made it worse that we're struggling with this, but it has exacerbated a problem that I think existed the whole time

insights.claim: Being able to open an agent and produce working code does not mean one should build in high-stakes domains — a non-specialist writing a bank's secure transaction process is the failure case — so core skills in architecture, security, business analysis and project management remain the gate on what gets built.
insights.speaker: Craig Smith
insights.so_what: Regulated-domain expertise retains scarcity value even as generic coding is commoditised — a durable differentiator for specialist consultancies and vendors.
insights.quote: just because I can do it doesn't mean I should do it

insights.claim: Domain knowledge and direct customer contact remain the prerequisite for both asking AI the right question and validating its output, so plain communication with customers is not displaced by AI.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Product discovery and customer research functions become more, not less, load-bearing as implementation cost falls toward zero.

themes.theme: Accountability Gap, Ethics and Environmental Cost

insights.claim: Accountability degrades mechanically as AI output volume rises — the more an organisation can build, the less it can understand — so a sense of responsibility for AI-written code has to be deliberately re-engineered.
insights.speaker: Vanessa Formicola
insights.so_what: The accountability gap is the sleeper regulatory and liability exposure in AI-generated software; controls and provenance become auditable requirements.
insights.quote: The more we can build, the less we can understand.

insights.claim: Professionals must remain accountable for delivered code whether or not AI wrote it, and 'it was AI, how could I know, it was one billion lines of code' cannot be allowed to function as a defence — which requires controls and well-structured harnesses that engineers can genuinely stand behind.
insights.speaker: Vanessa Formicola
insights.so_what: Expect harness/control-plane attestation to become the mechanism by which engineers and firms retain defensible accountability for agent output.
insights.quote: But it was AI. How could I know that? It was one billion lines of code

insights.claim: Engineers are using a tool that consumes large amounts of electricity and water and is more expensive than anything they have used before, on a planet already under strain, with no consensus answer on how to wield it without long-horizon damage.
insights.speaker: Shawna Martell
insights.so_what: Practitioner-level unease about AI's resource footprint is a leading indicator of internal green-software policies and procurement constraints on inference spend.
insights.quote: a tool that I understand is more expensive than maybe anything I've ever used before

insights.claim: Neuralwatt is cited as a startup that exposes open-source models such as GLM but prices them by power consumption rather than token count, claiming roughly 40% lower cost and making a user's environmental impact visible in the bill.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Power-based inference pricing is an emerging alternative billing primitive to tokens — watch whether major providers adopt it as energy costs become the binding constraint.
insights.quote: They expose open source models like GLM, but their pricing model is based on power consumption. And they claim something where you pay 40% less or something.

insights.claim: Token consumption is already a live proxy metric for the environmental impact of engineering work, but teams only notice it when they hit a quota or get reprimanded, echoing Jutta Eckstein's earlier call to treat environmental footprint as a measured metric.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Token/energy accounting is the ready-made hook for carbon reporting on AI workloads — a plausible next compliance surface for engineering orgs.
insights.quote: Now we're burning tokens. We have a metric right in front of us that's a proxy for the impact of the work we're doing.

insights.claim: Engineers routinely select premium models when a cheaper one would do, because the default behaviour is to reach for the biggest hammer rather than to be intentional about model choice.
insights.speaker: Rafiq Gemmail
insights.so_what: Undisciplined model selection inflates inference bills — model routing and cost-aware defaults are a concrete efficiency lever inside AI-heavy orgs.
insights.quote: And I see people picking the premium model sometimes when they shouldn't.

insights.claim: The offsetting upside case is that AI might solve nuclear fusion and eliminate the energy problem, or solve cancer and drive revolutions in healthcare, which would dominate the environmental cost.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: The bull case for tolerating AI's resource cost rests on unproven breakthrough outcomes — useful to name explicitly when assessing energy-vs-AI trade-off arguments.
insights.quote: what if AI solves nuclear fusion and then our energy problems are gone? What if AI solves cancer?

themes.theme: Creativity, Critical Thinking and Human Wellbeing

insights.claim: Every prior technology that collapsed creation cost — photography in visual art, parametric and generative design in architecture — triggered an explosion of creativity rather than displacing it, and AI should follow the same pattern in software.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: A reusable historical analogy for arguing that cheap generation expands rather than shrinks the market for creative output — relevant to any 'AI destroys the profession' thesis.
insights.quote: That unleashed a massive wave of creativity in the visual arts that led to abstract art, impressionism and all the amazing things that happened in visual arts after the invention of photography.

insights.claim: AI writes syntactically correct and often better code than an experienced ML engineer can, but frequently cannot produce creative solutions to problems, making creativity more valuable than ever.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: The scarce input shifts from implementation skill to problem framing and novel solution design — the skill to hire and pay for.
insights.quote: it can write syntactically correct code and very good code, probably better code than I can write, but can it come up with creative solutions to problems? I find often it can't

insights.claim: Constraints improve creativity, so removing the language and library debates that used to consume engineering attention frees teams to focus on solving the actual problem.
insights.speaker: Yinka Omole
insights.so_what: Standardisation on fewer languages and frameworks becomes a feature rather than a limitation in AI-assisted teams — consolidation pressure on niche tooling.
insights.quote: I think there has been proof that constraints can actually improve creativity.

insights.claim: A Harvard study this year found AI intensifies work for individuals rather than reducing it, and roughly 70-80% of people believe their role is at risk of being affected by AI, so teams are simultaneously more anxious and more overworked while still accelerating.
insights.speaker: Yinka Omole
insights.so_what: The productivity narrative and the labour-experience data point in opposite directions — burnout and attrition are the near-term realised cost of AI adoption.
insights.quote: there was the Harvard study earlier this year, which was showing that AI really intensifies work rather than reducing it for individuals

insights.claim: Harvard Business Review's June 2026 ranking of actual AI usage puts therapy and companionship at number one and astrology and tarot at number nine, while improving code and generating code fell from ranks five and eight in 2025 to ranks 78 and 69 — because mainstream adoption has swamped the technology industry's early lead, not because developers use AI less.
insights.speaker: Shane Hastie
insights.so_what: AI's centre of gravity has moved decisively to consumer and emotional use cases; developer tooling is now a small slice of a much larger usage base.
insights.quote: The number one use, therapy and companionship. Number nine, which worries me immensely, astrology and tarot readings.

insights.claim: The World Economic Forum's finding that society is losing the ability to think critically is being raised as a direct concern for software engineering, where critical thinking has long been formalised in disciplines like PMBOK, BABOK and testing practice.
insights.speaker: Shane Hastie
insights.so_what: Erosion of critical thinking is the mechanism by which AI adoption could reduce, rather than raise, decision quality in engineering orgs.
insights.quote: World Economic Forum saying we are losing the ability to think critically as a society.

insights.claim: The stated priority for the year ahead among senior practitioners is a shift from output and metrics toward quality, testing, robustness and human collaboration — building quickly is now easy, building something robust and valuable is not.
insights.speaker: Philip Mortimer
insights.so_what: Practitioner demand is rotating from generation tooling toward verification and quality tooling — the next budget line to expand.
insights.quote: You can build credibly quickly now, but are you building something that is robust and valuable?

insights.claim: Real innovation comes from people collaborating and talking to each other rather than from the output of AI tools, and work practices themselves must keep innovating alongside the technology.
insights.speaker: Craig Smith
insights.so_what: Process innovation is the lagging half of AI adoption; firms that only buy tools and leave practices unchanged capture the least value.
insights.quote: The real innovations come from people collaborating and talking to each other.
